items.label: f04-counterexample-first
items.front: What makes a good bug fix, per the counterexample method?
items.back: Name prior state, action and wrong observable result; turn the smallest counterexample into a failing test first; then strengthen the model (stable keys, focus restoration, serialized requests, graph traversal, rollback by temporary id) instead of special-casing the example.

items.label: f02-resume-is-untrusted
items.front: Why parse a saved multi-page session before resuming it?
items.back: Serialized browser data is untrusted input and the flow may have changed. Parse JSON, check page identities and value shapes, and fall back safely (undefined) instead of resuming into an impossible state.

items.label: f01-controlled-promises
items.front: How should you test debounced autosave for safety, not just for timing?
items.back: A controlled clock for the debounce, a controlled repository for version conflicts, and deferred promises resolved out of order for request races. A passing timer test does not prove overlapping requests are safe.

items.label: f03-validate-published-snapshot
items.front: Which form version should the server validate a submission against?
items.back: The immutable published snapshot the respondent saw, not whichever draft exists when the request arrives.

items.prompt: A submission commits but the response is lost, and the client retries with the same idempotency key. What does the repository return?

choices.text: The original submission, marked 'duplicate', with no second record
A 409 conflict, telling the client to generate a new key and submit again
A new submission, as a retry is always a new request with new answers
The original only if the answers are byte-identical, otherwise a second record

choices: The original submission, marked 'duplicate', with no second record
A 409 conflict, telling the client to generate a new key and submit again
A new submission, as a retry is always a new request with new answers
The original only if the answers are byte-identical, otherwise a second record

items.explanation: Retrying is correct only when the operation is idempotent: the client supplies a stable request key and the repository returns the original result for duplicate attempts.

items.prompt: Two branches from the current page both match the answers. Where does nextSession go?

choices.text: The next declared page, ignoring both branches
It throws an ambiguous-flow error and stays on the page
The branch whose target page is furthest ahead wins
The first matching branch in declaration order wins

choices: The next declared page, ignoring both branches
It throws an ambiguous-flow error and stays on the page
The branch whose target page is furthest ahead wins
The first matching branch in declaration order wins

items.explanation: Branch order is product behavior: flow.branches.find(...) picks the first match, else flow.pages[currentIndex + 1], else the session completes after the last page.

items.prompt: In the simulated autosave incident, an older save finished after a newer edit and showed stale state. Why did the 500 ms debounce not prevent it?

choices.text: The debounce delay was too short, and raising it to two seconds makes the older save finish first
Debounce limits when saves start, and it does not serialize requests already in flight
The browser cancelled the newer request as two fetches to the same URL were open at once
The server ignored the expected version, so any delay at all would have failed

choices: The debounce delay was too short, and raising it to two seconds makes the older save finish first
Debounce limits when saves start, and it does not serialize requests already in flight
The browser cancelled the newer request as two fetches to the same URL were open at once
The server ignored the expected version, so any delay at all would have failed

items.explanation: The fix chains writes on a queue, passes the latest accepted version to the next request, and lets only the newest request update visible state.

items.prompt: An optimistic comment is rendered with a temporary id and the server rejects it. What does a correct repair do?

choices.text: Retry the request automatically until the server accepts it
Remove it by its temporary id and put its text back for a retry
Refetch all comments, which hides the error and discards the text
Leave it visible with a pending badge until the page reloads

choices: Retry the request automatically until the server accepts it
Remove it by its temporary id and put its text back for a retry
Refetch all comments, which hides the error and discards the text
Leave it visible with a pending badge until the page reloads

items.explanation: The Sprint 13 flaw left a rejected comment pending forever; a deferred-then-rejected promise in the test exposes the missing rollback.

items.prompt: Why does the builder store only the selected field's id and look the field up during render?

choices.text: To make the selected field immutable while it is being edited
The id is needed for the URL, and the field object is too large to store
A copied field would need syncing after every edit or deletion
React state cannot hold objects, so the field must be stored as a string

choices: To make the selected field immutable while it is being edited
The id is needed for the URL, and the field object is too large to store
A copied field would need syncing after every edit or deletion
React state cannot hold objects, so the field must be stored as a string

items.explanation: Field list, settings and preview are three projections of one schema; a stored copy would go stale.

items.prompt: A respondent branches from page 1 straight to page 3, skipping page 2. Where does Back take them, and why?

choices.text: Nowhere, as Back is disabled after any branch
The completed screen, as Back after a branch ends the form
Page 1, as Back pops the actual visit history
Page 2, the previous element of the pages array

choices: Nowhere, as Back is disabled after any branch
The completed screen, as Back after a branch ends the form
Page 1, as Back pops the actual visit history
Page 2, the previous element of the pages array

items.explanation: nextSession appends the target page to visitedPageIds; backSession drops the last entry and returns to the new last one.

items.prompt: Why does the response cursor encode [submittedAt, id] and sort by id when timestamps tie?

choices.text: Ids are shorter than timestamps, which keeps the encoded cursor small enough for URLs
It makes newest-first and oldest-first sorts produce exactly the same order
The id encodes the page number, so the cursor can fall back to offset pagination
Timestamps can tie, and the id makes the order total so pages never skip or repeat

choices: Ids are shorter than timestamps, which keeps the encoded cursor small enough for URLs
It makes newest-first and oldest-first sorts produce exactly the same order
The id encodes the page number, so the cursor can fall back to offset pagination
Timestamps can tie, and the id makes the order total so pages never skip or repeat

items.explanation: A cursor says 'continue after this stable identity'; only a total order makes that identity unambiguous. Offset pagination fails differently, because N shifts when new responses arrive.

items.prompt: A respondent answers =HYPERLINK("http://x","a,b"). What does escapeCsvCell produce?

choices.text: The text with its commas removed and its quotes stripped before export
The raw text unchanged, as CSV treats none of these characters as special
An empty cell, as formula-like answers are dropped from the CSV export
A quoted cell with an apostrophe before the = and every inner quote doubled

choices: The text with its commas removed and its quotes stripped before export
The raw text unchanged, as CSV treats none of these characters as special
An empty cell, as formula-like answers are dropped from the CSV export
A quoted cell with an apostrophe before the = and every inner quote doubled

items.explanation: Leading = + - @ get an apostrophe prefix; any quote, comma or line break forces quoting with quotes doubled. CSV is a serialization format, not string joining.

items.prompt: A version diff compares fields by array position. A user only reorders two fields. What history does it report?

choices.text: Exactly one reorder, as the two field positions changed
A removal plus an addition, which teaches the wrong history
An error, as a position-based diff cannot handle any reorder
No change at all, as the field set is identical

choices: Exactly one reorder, as the two field positions changed
A removal plus an addition, which teaches the wrong history
An error, as a position-based diff cannot handle any reorder
No change at all, as the field set is identical

items.explanation: A position diff reports a pure reorder as a removal plus an addition; diffFormSchemas instead builds maps keyed by field.id, so a pure reorder reports no field removed, added or changed.

items.prompt: Request 1 and request 2 are queued by useAutosave and request 1 resolves 'saved' with version 5 after request 2 was created. What does the hook do with request 1's result?

choices.text: It keeps version 5 for the next save but does not update visible state, as request 1 is stale
It cancels request 2, as a newer save has already completed for the same schema
It shows 'Saved version 5' on screen first and then overwrites it when request 2 finishes
It discards version 5, so request 2 is sent with the older version and then hits a conflict

choices: It keeps version 5 for the next save but does not update visible state, as request 1 is stale
It cancels request 2, as a newer save has already completed for the same schema
It shows 'Saved version 5' on screen first and then overwrites it when request 2 finishes
It discards version 5, so request 2 is sent with the older version and then hits a conflict

items.explanation: Inside the queued callback, version.current is updated on 'saved', then the result returns early when requestId !== latestRequest.current; requests run one at a time on the promise chain.

items.prompt: Visibility rules make A depend on B, B on C and C on A. Each reference is a valid field id and no rule depends on itself. How does the validator catch this?

choices.text: The direct self-reference check, as A's dependencies eventually lead back to A
By counting dependencies and rejecting any field that depends on more than one
It does not, as valid ids guarantee a valid graph and the rule set is accepted
A DFS with visiting and visited sets finds a node already on the active path

choices: The direct self-reference check, as A's dependencies eventually lead back to A
By counting dependencies and rejecting any field that depends on more than one
It does not, as valid ids guarantee a valid graph and the rule set is accepted
A DFS with visiting and visited sets finds a node already on the active path

items.explanation: Valid node ids do not guarantee a valid graph; pairwise checks miss A → B → C → A, the counterexample in the flaw ledger. The fix strengthens the model with graph traversal.

items.prompt: A field's settings panel is expanded, then the field is moved up one row, and the expanded panel now appears on a different field. What was the planted flaw?

choices.text: Expanded state was saved to the URL and reloaded on the next render
Rows were keyed by array position instead of by the stable field.id
The panel read its field from a stale closure that useCallback would fix
The reducer swapped the wrong two fields, so the expanded one was the moved one

choices: Expanded state was saved to the URL and reloaded on the next render
Rows were keyed by array position instead of by the stable field.id
The panel read its field from a stale closure that useCallback would fix
The reducer swapped the wrong two fields, so the expanded one was the moved one

items.explanation: React identity is domain identity, not display position: the fix keys rows by field.id and restores focus by id, since the same Sprint 4 flaw also lost keyboard focus after a move.
